[540 C D] (iii)The testa tion test is not merely the intention of testator but also the intention of his mind. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letter was recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives the greatest that could be said is that he was in possession of the letters; (ii) the prosecution has only proved that the appellant was in possession and that he was not in exclusive possession of the articles seized from the house in question; and (iii) the prosecution failed to establish that the appellant had acquired knowledge or reason to believe that the articles were stolen property. 1378: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujgar Singh regarding the appellant ' having given a false account of the incident and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to prove that the appellant committed the murder of Sheo Sahal. 3168: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1956 and its shareholders were directors. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the Companies Act, 1913 were filed before the Registrar of Companies on 30 10 1967. The balance sheets and profit and losses account of the Company as required by section 220(2) of the Act were filed before this Court on 30 10 1968. The appellant company had been prosecuted for breaches of sections 32 and 131 of the Companies ' Act, 1913 and section 220(3) of the . The High Court held that since no balance sheet was laid before the company in general meeting before it could be said to have contravened section 134 of the Companies. Act, 1913, the appellant company was liable to be punished under section 134 of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the view taken by the High Court was contrary to the language used in sections 32 and 132 of the Companies, Act, 1913. HELD: (i) Section 131 of the Act provides that a person charged with an offence cannot rely on his default as an answer to the charge and so, if he is responsible for not calling the general body meeting and to lay the balance sheet and profits and loss account before it may expose him to punishment under other provisions of the Act. [639 B] (ii) The expression "in any case" in section 131 of the Company Act, 1913 does not make any difference to the decision of the case. It merely means that the person charged should have acted honestly or reasonably in the discharge of his duty. If he has acted honestly, he must be deemed to have committed an offence under section 134. [640 C D] (iii) The words "in any such case" in the proviso to section 131 are wide enough to include cases where the company itself has not been able to show that the failure to comply with the requirements of section 220 was due to any deliberate act or omission on the part of the company. [641 A B]
4568: The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Central Health Service on September 9, 1966. The appellant was not only holding the post of Radiologist in the said hospital but was also actively associated with teaching the under graduate and post graduate students as an Associate Professor of the said hospital. The appellant had been working as a Professor since July 1, 1973 till his substantive appointment in the said post. The appellant 's case is that he was entitled to be considered for promotion as Professor in the said specialist grade because he was a candidate for the post in question. The appellant contended that the post of Assistant Professor in the specialist grade fell vacant in 1973 and the recruitment rules were not framed till the year 1963. The appellant further contended that the Rules were not framed until the year 1964. The appellant submitted that the Rules could not have been made retrospective. The High Court held that the Rules had been framed in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution and therefore they could not have retrospective effect. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Rules do not contemplate any selection or consultation with the Public Service Commission. They are merely administrative instructions and cannot override the statutory provisions. [26F] 1.2 The Rules do provide for the manner in which the posts are to be filled up. The method of filling up the posts is provided in Rule 8(a) and (b). The Rules do no expressly exclude the method of recruitment prescribed in Rule 8. The Rules do nothing more than make it obligatory for the appointing authority to frame the Rules in consultation with the Commission. [27B C] 1.3 The Rules do neither require the Public Service Commissions to consult the Commission nor do they lay down any guidelines for the purpose of making appointments to the posts. The Rules are merely advisory in nature and do not confer any right upon the candidates who are selected by the Commission. The Rules have to be read together and the word "consultation" has to be given its full meaning
2440: The appellant company was a small scale industry in the State of Orissa. It had two units, one at the Titaghur Paper Mill and the other at the J.K. 5364: The respondent was appointed as an Assistant Administrative Officer in the Life Insurance Corporation of India on 1st September, 1956. The Corporation challenged the order before the High Court which held that the order of retirement was not a punishment and accordingly quashed it. The Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Corporation is an independent entity and its employees are not liable to be retrenched except under the provisions of section 25F of the Act. [841 B] (2) The Corporation has no employee of its own to carry on the vast business of the large number of insurers which had been taken over by it. In order to meet the requirement of section 11 of the Act came into existence. Held, that the provisions contained in sections 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Act are not violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and are not hit by article 14 of Constitution. The provisions are intended to provide a machinery for investigation and report by the Commission and the Commission has to make recommendations as to whether there should be any further inquiry or investigation. 2207: The respondent was a dealer in the business of sale and purchase of goods. He purchased certain goods from the appellant who was the sole proprietor of the business. The sales tax authorities found that the respondent had sold the goods to another person who had no title to it. The Sales Tax Officer, however, held that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title. The respondent appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner as well as to the Board of Revenue but the appeals were dismissed. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of assessment passed by the Sales Tax Authorities and the Board of Revising Authority. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the respondent being a dealer in respect of the transactions of sale took place before the transfer of the business under Rule 21 A of the Rules framed in exercise of the powers conferred on the State Government by section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent was not entitled to be assessed to sales tax on the transaction of sale which took place before him. [801 B] 2. The respondent could not be made liable for payment of sales tax on his own account. The liability to pay sales tax is not dependent upon the transfer of ownership or the transfer of possession. [802 C D] 3. The respondent cannot be said to have been made liable for arrears of sales tax because he had no title over the property. [803 E F] 4. The respondent had no right to recover the arrears of sales Tax from the respondent. The respondent has no right to claim any interest on the amount of arrears of sales Taxes. [804 G H] 5. The respondent having failed to make out a case for the grant of relief under article 226, the High Court should not have granted the same relief to the respondent. [805 A B] 6. The respondent 's contention that the respondent could not recover the arrears from the respondent was without substance. The respondent did not have any right to recover any amount from the respondent as the respondent had no title. [806 C D]

The plaintiffs ' case was that as a result of a letter written by the Inspector of Mines on August 18, 1941, the plaintiffs made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The defendants denied that they had encroached on their coal mines. The plaintiffs also contended that the defendants did not have any right to claim compensation for the alleged encroachment. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that they had knowledge of the defendants ' encroachment. The High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the burden of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the defendants was on the appellants. It was further contended that the High Courts had wrongly held that the onus of proof to prove the existence of the alleged encroachment lay on the defendants. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court has given the finding on the assumption that the initial burden was on the defendants to prove that the defendants have knowledge of the alleged encroachments. [539 E] (2) The High Courts had rightly held that the burden was on them to prove that there was no encroachment on the land. [540 A B] (3) The High courts had correctly held that the evidence led by the parties showed that the defendants were in possession of the land in dispute and that they had been dispossessed by the defendants. [541 C D] (4) The High court was justified in holding that there was nothing on record to show that the defendants ever took any steps to dispossess the plaintiffs. [542 F]

3924: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. It is well settled that if two views are possible, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the two views. [366B] 2.1 The High Court should have considered the evidence in its proper perspective and come to a conclusion which would be consistent with the innocence of the accused. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his removal from office on the ground that he had been removed from his office without obtaining the previous sanction of the President under clause (c) of sub section 1 of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant could not be prosecuted for having committed the offence of criminal misconduct as contemplated by clause (e) of sub sec. 1 of section5 of the Prevention o f Corruption Act, 1988. The appellant appealed to this Court against the judgment of the High Cour t. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A Judge of the High court can be removed from his post only by an order of the President passed after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and in a case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice may appoint a person who is or has been a Judge of a High Court to act as a Judge in his place. [801F G] 1.2 In the present case, the appellant was appointed as Judge of the Delhi High Court by an Order dated March 31. 1970. The question whether the appellant could be removed from the post of Judge of the Court of the Supreme Cou rt arose out of the fact that the President had not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge of that Court even though the President had approved the appointment of the appellant as a Judge. [802B D] 1.3 The High Court was wrong in holding that the President did not have the power to remove him from his office. [803E F] 1.4 The High Court erred in law in holding that it was not competent to the President to remove a judge of the High Courts merely because he was a Judge. [804A B] 1.5 The High Court should have taken into account
2124: The appellant was a member of the Sahas. He claimed to belong to a Scheduled Caste in West Bengal. His case was that he belonged to a smaller caste group and that it was not a Schedule Caste. The respondent contested the election on the ground that he belonged a Scheduled Caste. The Tribunal rejected his claim, but the High Court held that the respondent 's case was not one of a Schedule Caste and that the appellant was not entitled to be declared elected. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was not a member of a Scheduled Caste within the meaning of article 332 of the Constitution. [380 G] (ii) The appellant had no right to challenge the validity of the order of the High Court rejecting his prayer for declaring him elected. [381 D] (iii) The appellant could not be said to belong to the Schedule Caste specified in item 40 of Part I of the Schedule to the Order which set out the Scheduled Castes in West Bengal as the Scheduled Castes specified in item 39 of Part I thereof. [383 E F] (iv) The appellant did not fall within the purview of the expression "Scheduled Castes" in article 341 of the Constitution and therefore did not fall under any of the sub clauses of that article. [384 A B] (v) The appellant cannot be said to be a member of an independent caste which is included in the Schedule to article 366(24). [385 C]
78: The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for receiving a sum or consideration as a condition for the reli quishment of his tenancy. He was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 30,000. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one day simple imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (a) the word "relinquishment" in section 18(2) of the Act meant only an act of relinquishment and not a relinquishment; (b) the word 'revocation ' used in the section did not include a relinquishment and (c) the wordings in the section were intended to convey a different meaning than the word 'discharge ' in section 19(2). HELD: (1) The word "rellevant" in section 19 is used in the same sense in section 18 (1) of Act 1 of 1956. [423 E] (2) The word 'relinquish ment ' in section 18 means only an act by which a person obtains possession of the premises on behalf of another. It does not mean anything more than an act by the latter. [424 A B]

Its work force consists of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. They served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant, and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. 314: The appellant was put up for trial before a Magistrate of the First Class, Patiala, who convicted him under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code. He was acquitted by the Sessions Judge and the High Court on appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary when the act complained of was done while the accused was actually engaged in the performance of his official duties; (ii) the prosecution having been launched without any sanction under section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court; and (iii) the order of acquittal passed by the trial Magistrate was illegal as sanction had not been obtained under section 197 (1) of Code of Criminal procedure. HELD: (i) The question whether sanction under section197(1) is necessary when the acts complained of were committed while the accused person was actually engaged or employed in the performance 'of his official duties was one which could be said to have been done while the public servant was actually engaged, and the question whether sanction was necessary under section 197 of the Code was one of fact depending upon the facts of each case. [1305 B C] (2) The question as to whether sanction under Section 197(1), Cr. P.C., was necessary when an act was done while a public servant was engaged in the discharge of his official duty was one which would fall within the scope of the duties of a public servant if he was actually engaged. [1306 D E] (3) The question of sanction under section 204(1) Cr. P., Code of Criminal Proc edure, was not a matter of law but a mixed question of fact and law. It was open to the appellant to raise this point at the time of the hearing of the appeal. [1307 G H]
2122: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961 and was incorporated in 1961. In 1962, the Company Law Board issued an order under section 237(b) of the appointing persons as Inspectors for investigating the affairs of the company. The order was challenged by the appellant company on the ground that it was made mala fide; that the order was made mala fides; and that the order had been made with a view to defraud its creditors, members or any other person. The High Court held that the order being mala fide, the same could not be done without giving the appellant an opportunity to show cause why it should not be made. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order is made mala fide. It is not necessary that there must be some material to justify the making of the order. [560 D] (2) The order was made by the Chairman of the Board who was the competent authority to make the order. The order having been made by the chairman of the Board, he was bound to give the appellant an adequate opportunity to show that the business of the company was being conducted with intent to defraud the creditors, members and any other person, or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose. [540 C D] (3) The order being mala fides, the same cannot be said to have been made mala fide merely because it was made at the instance of the shareholders. [541 A B] (4) The order has been made mala fides. [542 E F] (5) The order does not suffer from any infirmity. [543 G H]
2796: The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment. They were convicted on the sole evidence of having in their possession pieces of cloth which were later identified to belong to the traders. In appeal, the High Court acquitted them but maintained the convictions and sentences awarded by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the circumstances under which the one presumption or the other may be drawn should not have been drawn since the circumstances do not admit the drawing of such a presumption; (ii) the recovery of the fruits of crime itself is not proved as the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt; (iii) the recovery from the house of the appellants was not proved because they had no opportunity to see the articles recovered from them; (iv) the recovery was made from a place where there was no electricity and the police could not have arrested the appellants without the aid of a public servant; (v) the recovery cannot be said to have been made from a person who was merely present at the scene of occurrence and was not connected with the commission of the offence; (vi) the recovery is not proved because the witnesses did not identify the accused persons. HELD: (1) The circumstances under which an inference can be drawn are those which are inconsistent with the innocence of the accused and are reasonably probable on the basis of which the appellate courts shall draw the inference that the accused committed the offence. [675 B] (2) The circumstance that the appellant was absconding for a long time and was found in his house at the time of the dacoity does not mean that he must have been in the company of the dacoits. It is only when the appellant is found absconding that he can be held guilty of the offence. If the appellant was not available for trial and was not produced before the Magistrate, the fact that he was absconding would not make him liable to punishment. [676 C D]
2649: The appellants were partners of a firm registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. They carried on business as commission agents and stockists in Bombay. In the accounting year ending 31st March, 1952, the appellants had paid a sum of Rs. 2,68,385/ to the firm for the purchase of certain goods. The firm was dissolved on 1st April, 1953. The appellants claimed that the debt of Rs.2,68, 385/ due to them was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending business. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim holding that the debt did not arise in the course of the appellants ' business as chemists and druggist nor in the course.of their money lending business, and that the debt was not a loss sustained in the other business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The Tribunal held that the debt in question was not a good and doubtful debt and that it was not a debt representing loss sustained in other business. On reference, the High Court answered the question against the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The debt of Rs.. 2,68.385/ was not a business or profession but a liability arising out of a contract entered into by the firm with the appellants. [808 B] (ii) The debt was not an asset within the meaning of section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, as in force at the relevant time. It was not a liability arising from a contract entered by the firm in which the appellants were partners. [809 C D] (iii) The debt in question is not a bad debt in the sense that it does not represent any loss sustained in any other business. It is only a contingent liability which can be brought to tax. [810 E F] (iv) The debt is not a debt in the nature of a debt within the meaning Of section 10(1) (xv). It is a liability in respect of a transaction which has been entered into by a person who is not a party to the transaction. [811 A B] (v) The debt cannot be said to have arisen in the course whereof the debt was contracted
2052: The respondents who were employed in the appellant bank, were employed in banks which were not governed by the Sastry award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. They claimed that they should be fitted in the new scales of pay fixed by the appellant bank under para 5.356 of the Desai award as modified and that they should also be fitted in a new scale of pay. The respondents contended that they had been wrongly fitted in the revised scale of pay and that their pay should have been fixed at the same stage in the new scale applicable to them under the Desai award. Held, that the respondents ' basic pay as on 31st January 1960 shall not be reduced in any case. The respondents were entitled to be fitted in an appropriate scale of pay provided by the Desai award and that they could not be fitted in any other scale of pay than those prescribed by the Desai. The respondents had no right to be fitted into the new scales. The respondents could only be fitted in such a scale of pay as was prescribed by the tribunal.
5266: The appellants were the owners of a piece of land in Calcutta. They purchased it from the State of West Bengal for a consideration of Rs. 1,00,000. The State Government sanctioned a scheme for construction of a five star hotel. The appellants applied to the State Government for permission to construct a five stars hotel. The State refused to grant the permission on the ground that the land was not suitable for the purpose. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the refusal of the State Government to grant the land. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the decision taken by the State Government was neither unreasonable nor arbitrary and that taking away of four acres of land from the Zoo was not unreasonable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the decision of the State was not arbitrary or unreasonable; (ii) the decision was not mala fide; (iii) the decision had been taken without any basis; and (iv) the decision is vitiated by non application of mind. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The decision of the Government is not unreasonable. It is an administrative act. [801 G] (2) The decision taken by a public authority is not open to challenge on the ground of arbitrariness. [802 A B] (3) The decision has to be based on objective criteria. The decision must have some rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved. [803 C D] (4) The decision is not arbitrary but is made after considering relevant factors. [804 E F] (5) The decision cannot be said to be arbitrary if it is based on irrelevant considerations or material particularised in the impugned order. [805 A B]
5248: The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. He had two sons, one of whom was a Hindu Undivided Family and the other a Hindu Understanding. In the assessment year 1957 58 he claimed that the gift made by him in his favour was not valid gifts as it did not have cash balance of Rs.4000 only on 1st January, 1957. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the gift was invalid because the donee had not made any provision for the payment of cash or for the return of the amount to the donee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The Tribunal held that the gift in question was invalid because it was not supported by cash. On reference, the High Court held that the donee could not be said to have made any provision in the books of account for the purpose of making an advance from the bank. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The gift in question is not a gift in the sense of a transfer of property within the meaning of section 2(6A)(c) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [125B] (2) The gift was not a gift simpliciter but was a transaction which was intended to be used for the benefit of the donor. It was not a mere transaction of sale. [126C D] (3) The gift is not a transfer of the ownership of the donor but is merely a device to make the gift effective. [127E] (4) The gift has been made by the donor in favour of the donee who had no interest in the property. The gift is therefore not a gift of the nature described in section 2(7) of the Act. [127F]
2304: The appellant was appointed as a District Judge in the Orissa Superior Judicial Service. He was transferred to the Orissa Super Time Judicial Service. In October 1966, he was posted as a district judge and was promoted as a district judges. On November 10, 1966, the High Court issued an order transferring him from one post to another. The High Court directed that the appellant should be retained in his original post of district judge for a period of three years or till the date on which he would have attained the age of superannuation whichever is earlier. The appellant challenged this order by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High court dismissed the petition holding that the transfer of the appellant was not made by the Governor but was made by the High Court as part of the control vested in it by article 235. The High 'Court held that the power to transfer a district judge from one post or cadre to another was not vested in the High Court under article 233. The High. Court also held that the transfer was not made under article 235. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court had no power to transfer the appellant from one post/cadre to another. [801 G] (2) The High Courts were competent to issue directions regarding transfers of officers and employees of the State Government. [802 A B]
6881: The appellant was the owner of a piece of land in village Mouza Mouza Gobindpur, District Burdwan. He sold it to one M/s. Baijnath Singh, who was the purchaser from the respondent. The sale deed recited that the land was purchased by the appellant for a consideration of Rs. 1,000/ and that the price was fixed at Rs. 2,500/ per acre. The appellant claimed that he had purchased the land under a registered sale deed dated January 28, 1959, which contained a condition that the vendor should pay the price of the land within 15 days of the date of the sale. The vendor contended that the sale was invalid as the vendor did not have the right to sell the land. The trial court held that the sale deed was invalid because the vendor did no have the right of pre emption on the land. On appeal the High Court upheld the decision of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sales were void as they were made without notice to the vendor and were not binding on him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The sale is valid and not infringe any Article 14 or Article 19(1)(f). The sale is not void as it is not made by the vendor but is made by the vendee. [124F] (2) The sale was not vitiated by fraud or undue influence. The sale was made by the appellant with his consent. The appellant could not be said to have been prejudiced by the fact that the sale is void. [125A] (3) The sale in question was not vitiated merely because the vendor had not the right of predecisional hearing before the sale was effected. [126B C] (4) The sale being void ab initio, the appellant could not claim any right of preemption. [127C]
6668: The appellant, who was the father of the respondent No. 1 and his two sons, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his share in the property. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated by the compromise decree. The appellate court confirmed the decree. In second appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the amount of Rs.1,00,000/as stipulated in the compromise decree and directed the trial court to pay the balance of Rs.50,000/to the respondent No 1. The High Court further directed that the amount of interest should be paid within one month from the date of the judgment. The alienees were also given liberty to apply for modification of the decree. The alienee respondent No. 2 filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 C.P.C. for setting aside the sale deed dated 21.8.1987 executed by the appellant in favour of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. The said application was dismissed by the trial court. The High court allowed the revision petition filed by the alienees and set aside the order of the appellate court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The compromise decree passed by the trial Court is binding on the alienees. [901H; 902A] 2. The alienation made by the alienors is valid and binding on the parties. [903B] 3. The alienations are valid and the transferees have become owners of the property. [904E] 4. The alienated properties are not liable to be sold or disposed of in any manner whatsoever. [905F] 5. The alienators shall deliver vacant possession of the property by 30th April, 1991, to Seshiah and in the event of failure to do so the trial court is directed by our present order to deliver vacant possession to Seshia. [906G H]
415: The appellant was detained under the Bombay Police Act, 1951. He challenged his detention on the grounds that (1) the order of detention was made without any real application of mind by the detaining authority, and (2) the grounds furnished in this case were vague and lacking in material particulars. Held, that the order of the detention was not based on any material whatever but was based on conjecture and surmises. It was not a mere formality; it was an attempt to suppress the freedom of the appellant to ventilate his point of view on the Goan Politics and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos. The order of detention did not contain any reference to the fact that the appellant had been supplied with the grounds of detention. The non supply of the grounds would vitiate the order of preventive detention. The order was therefore invalid. State vs Mask & Co., [1955] 1 S.C.R. 771, relied on.
2248: The appellant was a Panchayat under the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958. The Panchayat passed resolution No. 2 with a view to levy octroi duty on the goods coming within its local limits as per the Schedule 1 of the Rules. On July 14, 1961, the Panchayat passed resolution no. 5 which reads as follows: "5. The matter of levying octroi duty shall be undertaken in accordance with the Panchayat Act and its rules. The matter is being examined by the appropriate authority. " The appellant filed an appeal before the Panchayat Samiti against the order of the Panchayat. The Panchayat Samiti allowed the appeal and set aside the order of assessment. The Panchayat also directed that the octroi nakas should be got fixed from the appellant. The Panchayat appealed to the State Government. The State Government dismissed the appeal. The Panchayat preferred an appeal to the State Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the appeal was barred by limitation. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Standing Committee had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal on merits as the appeal to the Panchayat Samiti was barred by time. [801 G] (ii) The Standing Committees had no jurisdiction or power to decide the appeals on merits. The Panchayat could not have decided the appeals on the merits. [802 A B] (iii) The Standing committee had no jurisdiction in deciding the appeal on the merits as the appeals were barred by limitation; and (iv) The appellant was not importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat as per the schedule. [803 C D] (v) The Standing Commis sioner had no jurisdiction whatsoever to decide the case on merits as it had failed to fix the octroi naka. [804 E F] (vi) The Standing Commi tions had no jurisdiction over the matter. [805 H]
5142: The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was a dangerous person within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Act. The order of detention was confirmed by the State Government and the detenu was served with the grounds of detention. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of detention. A Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the writ petition without any speaking order. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of the detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The order passed by the District Magistrate is not an order of preventive or punitive nature but is one made under section 3 (2) of 'the Act. [910E] 1.2. The order does not indicate that the detaining authority had considered the question whether the detenu should be released or not. It merely states that the detaining officer has formed the opinion that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the detenu is likely to be released from custody in the near future. [911F G] 1.3. The order cannot be said to have indicated that the detaining authorities were satisfied that the detenu was likely to be enlarged on bail. [912A B] 1.4. The order is not an ordinary order of preventive action. It is not an interlocutory order. [913C D] 1.5. The order must show that the detaining authori ties had applied their mind to the relevant facts and material before them. [914D E] 1.6. The order can be said to contain some reasons which may not be exhaustive or elaborate. But the fact that the detaining aut hority had recorded its satisfaction that the detenu would continue to indulge in prejudicial activities and that he was likely to continue his nefarious activities, is not sufficient to justify the passing of the order. [991G H] 1.7. The order in the instant case does not disclose that the detaining Author ity had applied its mind
2065: The appellants were the trustees of a temple in which the respondents were appointed as trustees. They had been granted a certificate under section 87 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, for possession of the properties in suit. The respondents filed an application before the Magistrate claiming that the properties in question belonged to them on the basis that they were the owners of the said properties. The Magistrate held that the respondents had proved their title to the properties in dispute and directed them to deliver possession of the same. The appellants preferred an appeal against this order to the District Munsif who remanded the case to him with directions to deliver possession to the respondents. The District Munsif dismissed the appeal holding that the respondents could not be said to have acquired title to the property by adverse possession. The respondents then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the correctness of the decision of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order of the Magistrate holding that the appellants had failed to establish their title to any part of the properties covered by the grant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the decision of a court is conclusive only when there are two possible interpretations of the words in a statute; (ii) where the words of a statute are clear and unambiguous, the courts should give effect to the intention of the legislature and the onus of proving that the law does not discriminate between different persons or things is on the person who seeks to sustain his claim. It was further submitted that the respondents having succeeded in the appeal, the appellants must be deemed to have become the owners of all the properties covered in the grant. HELD: (1) The decision of the High Court cannot be sustained because the respondents did not prove their title to these properties. [877 C] (2) The respondents had established their title to certain properties on the basis of the grant made by the manager of a temple. The respondents had also produced evidence to show that the original grant had been made on the basis, that the original grantee had accepted the grant and that he had transferred the properties to the appellants. [878 D E]
4641: The appellants, who were partners of a partnership firm, applied to the District Magistrate for permission to construct a modern Cinema Hall at the Apsara Theatre. The District Magistrate granted the permission on July 22, 1969, under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989, to the appellants to erect a modern cinema hall in the Apsra Theatre, which was the subject matter of the licence. The appellants challenged the grant of the licence by the District Magistrate before the High Court contending that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsar Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor dated December 29, 1977, which was confirmed in appeal by the State Government and which had acquired finality between the parties by reason of the dismissal of the writ petition and the Special Leave Petition by the High Court and Supreme Court. The appellants contended that the renewal was not necessary since the licence was issued by the District magistrate under section 3(1)(b) of the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The High Court held that the renewal could not be done in the name 'of any party other then the original licensee '. The appellants filed an appeal against this order of the High Court before the Supreme Court. In the appeal, the appellants contended that they had no locus standi to challenge the grant of licence and that the renewal should have been refused because the appellants had not been able to establish their case that the renewal application was not maintainable. The appellants are not entitled to challenge the validity of the renewal of their licence. [914A] 4. 380: The appellants were displaced persons, and on 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to them under section 7 of the Act calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled. The appellants replied that they had breached the terms of the agreement and called upon them to pay the arrears of rent within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notice and prayed for an order quashing the notice. Held, that the notice was valid and the Custodian had power to cancel the lease in respect of the mills and the factory. The order passed by the Custodian was not without jurisdiction as it was made without jurisdiction. The order was bad because the Custodian had no power to cancel it. The order did not affect the rights of the appellants which were protected by the provisions of the Act. The order could not be challenged on the ground that it affected the rights of any person other than the Custodian. The order merely directed the Custodian to take possession of the mills or the factory and to put the appellants in possession thereof.
7109: The appellant was a minor son of one Raghubir Singh who died in the year 1976. He had two sons, namely, Smt. Savitri Devi and Smt. Sita Devi. The land in question was purchased by his father in the year 1957. The land was inherited by his mother from her husband. The appellant filed a revision application before the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan challenging the order of the Sub Divisional Officer dated 5th May, 1976 passed under Section 230 of the Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973. The Board held that Surendrapal Singh, (appellant) aged about 725 years, was a minor and used to 726 study in Punjab and Haryana and therefore, could not be said to be a major son of Raghubir singh. The Board further held that the land in possession of the appellant was ancestral. The Board also held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief as he did not have any right to claim partition or allotment of land. The Board, however, set aside the order of Sub Divisional Officer and remanded the case to the Sub Divisional officer for deciding the matter afresh after hearing the parties. The Board of Revenue dismissed the revision petition filed by the appellant against the order of remand passed by the Board. The High Court allowed the writ petitions filed by the respondents and set aside the orders of the Board of Revenuer. Hence these appeals by special leave. 5538: The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. 1762: The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the merger of the former State into the Matsya Union. He applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni with which he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. His case further was that though he asked the State for refund of this advance duty, the State did not pay back the same to him. In the meantime, rapid constitutional changes took place after August 15, 1947. The respondent applied for and obtained a permit for import of 15,500 maunds from the customs department of the State of Rajasthan. The appellant refused to accept the permit on the ground that the respondent had already paid the amount of Rs. 30.000/ as export duty in the year 1947. The appellant contended that the respondent was liable to meet the liability under article 295(2) of the Constitution and other provisions made during the period when mergers were taking place after August, 15, 1947 and that the State of Madhya Pradesh was bound by the obligation of the former to pay the amount of the permit. Held, that the respondent could not be said to have been guilty of breach of any fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(1)(g) of the constitution. The respondent was not entitled to claim any relief under article 32 of the Constitution. The respondent had no right to ask for a writ of mandamus or direction against the State of Matsya to discharge its liability under article 32. The respondent could not invoke article 32 of his own wrong. The petition was misconceived and should be dismissed.
652: The appellants in the three appeals and others were carrying on business in cotton and groundnut. They filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, as amended by the Madras General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1953, and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Act and the Rules constituted an unreasonable restriction upon the appellants ' fundamental right to carry on business and that they did not contravene article 19(1)(g). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the impugned Act and the rules were invalid because they infringed articles 14 and 19(1) (g) of the Constitution; that the Act was discriminatory inasmuch as it prohibited persons who were having a licence to purchase or sell agricultural produce and that the Act imposed no restrictions on the appellants ' right to do business within the notified area. Held, that the Act is valid and the Rules made thereunder are valid. The Act does not infringe any fundamental right guaranteed under article 19(l)(g) of Constitution. It is only when the Act imposes reasonable restrictions that the State can impose such restrictions. The Act is not intended to be used as a shield against arbitrary legislation. The Act has been enacted with a view to regulate the buying and selling of commercial crops and to provide for the regulation of their sale and purchase of such commercial crops. The Act provides for the regulation and control of the buying and/or selling of commercial crop and the regulation of its sale and purchase thereof. The Act also prohibits persons who do business in cotton, groundnut and groundnuts. The Act therefore creates a reasonable restriction on the petitioners ' fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(I)(g) and makes them subject to the same restrictions which are imposed by section 3 of the Act.

2657: The appellant was the plaintiff in a suit for recovery of money. He had obtained an order of injunction restraining encashment of the letters of credit pending disposal of the suit. The High Court granted him interim injunction. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the order granting interim injunction did not amount to a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding and therefore the order was not a final order within the meaning of article 133(1) of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The expression "final order" is used in section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, section 109 of the Code of Civil Procedure and article 133(2) of the constitution. [701 G] (ii) A final order passed by the High Court does not amount to any final decision on a matter which is directly and substantially in issue in a suit. It is only when the final order decides the question involved in the suit or proceeding that the right of the parties can be said to have been finally determined. [702 B C] (iii) An order of stay passed under section 19 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1899, cannot be regarded as a final decision within the meaning Of article 133(3) of the Con stitution. [703 D E] (iv) The order of the High Court was not final but was merely an interlocutory order. The order of stay was not final. [704 F] (v) The order granting interim injunctions was not a judgment or decree. The order was not final and could not be challenged in a civil court. [705 H]
4807: The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti on April 1, 1975. He was promoted as a Head clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974. On April 1, 1976 he was promoted as an officiating Head Clerk. On April 2, 1975, the appellant was appointed to officiate as a Head Cashier. On April 3, 1975, he was promoted to officiate in the post of a Head Clerk. In July 1973, the appellant came to be appointed as a head cashier and was working as a Head cashier. On March 14, 1975, a resolution was passed by the Panchayat Samiti that the appellant should be absorbed in Government service as a clerk. The appellant was not given any opportunity to show cause against his reversion. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions as were applicable to him prior to his absorption in the Panchayat. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion to the post of Head Clerk on the date on which he was appointed as such. [737F] 1.2 The appellant was promoted as Head Clerk on an adhoc basis in January, 1974, or the further fact that he was appointed to the post on April 1.1975, but he was reverted to his original position on April 1 and continued to work as a Head Assistant till he was absorbed in the Panchayat Samiti. The fact that the appellant was promoted to the post in January 1974, or July 1973, is irrelevant for the purpose of judging whether the appellant was entitled for being considered for promotion. [738E F] 1.3 The appellant was rightly held entitled to be absorbed in the post in which he was working on the date of his appointment as a Head Clerks. [739G] 1.4 The appellant was never given any notice of termination of his services nor was he given any opportunity of showing cause against his termination. His case was governed by the provisions of section 35(3) of the Act. [740A B]
4451: The appellant was the Mahant of a Math. He had two wives, one of whom was a Hindu and the other a Hindu. The appellant 's case was that he was entitled to the exemption from income tax under section 10(2) (xv) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 10(1)(xv). The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Assistant Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the fund was personal property of the Math and therefore the burden lay upon the appellant to prove that the income from the trust funds was his personal property. HELD: (i) The appellant could not be said to have acquired any personal property in his possession. The mere fact that a person is an ascetic does not raise any presumption that a property in his occupation is his personal property or that he has acquired any personal income. [875 G] (ii) The appellant was entitled to exemption under section 10 (1)(xv) of Act, 1922, because he was the Mahants and members of the Math. The income from the properties belonging to the Math was received by him as a trustee for the Math. It was not his personal property but was the personal property of a Hindu. [876 B C] (iii) The appellant had no personal property at all. His claim to exemption from income Tax was based on the fact that he was the trustee for the math. The appellant was not the beneficiary of the trust. The income derived from the properties belonged to the Math. [877 D E]
1181: The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village Raikot in 1949. They made an application for consolidation of their lands with those of the appellants in the village. The appellants were allotted quasi permanent plots in lieu of their land acquired under the provisions of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General which was dismissed on July 23, 1960. The appellants preferred a revision application to the Custodian General. The Custodian General rejected the revision application on the ground that no land was available in the village in view of the cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the order dated October 31, 1952. The appellants then moved the High Court for a writ quashing the orders of the Custodian General and the Custodian General but the High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order of the Custodian was not a final order and that the appellants could not be said to have been deprived of any right of allotment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order passed by the Custodian General was not a speaking order and that it did not give any reasons for its conclusions. HELD: (i) The order of the Additional Custodian was not one of the grounds on which the order of cancellation of allotment was set aside. [336 G] (ii) The order passed by him was not a mere formality or a non-speaking order. It was open to the Custodian to consider whether the order of his predecessor was a speaking order or not. [337 A B] (iii) The order was not a reasoned order. The order merely stated that the allotment of land was cancelled. The order did not say that the allotment was cancelled. Nor did it say that the land was available for allotment. [338 C D] (iv) The order did nothing more than merely stating that the allotment had been cancelled. [339 E] (v) The order does not show that the allotment has been cancelled. The allotment is not cancelled. [360 F] (vi) The order merely states that the allotment is cancelled. [341 H]
3292: The appellant was the Mahant of a Dera. He died on 13 10 1970 leaving behind him his legal representatives. The respondent, who was the Mahants of the Dera, filed an application for bringing on record his legal representatives within the period prescribed under Rule 10(2) of the Civil Procedure Code. The trial Court held that the appellant had no knowledge about the date of death of the respondent and held that he was not entitled to bring on record his heirs as his legal representatives in view of the provisions of Order 22, rule 10 of the Code. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant could not be said to have been aware of the date of the death of the deceased respondent as he was not impleaded within the period provided by the Code. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the appeal had abated because the appellant had not taken steps to substitute his legal representatives and that the appeal should be allowed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appeal must be deemed to have abated against the appellant since he was not brought on record within the period of limitation prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure. [812E] 2. The right which the appellant claims to inherit is a right conferred upon him by the law of succession governing him. The right to sue survives where there are two or more persons claiming rights in the property of the deceased. The right of the appellant to sue survives only if he has notice of the death. [813F G] 3. The appellant was not impleaded as a party in the suit. His interest in the suit devolved upon the appellant as he was elected to be the Mahant. The appellant did not take any step to implead him as a party. The appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal. [814A B] 4. The appellant could not claim to be the legal representative of the deceased defendant. The appellant cannot claim to be a person interested in the estate of the deceased and therefore, Order 22, r. 10 would not apply. [815C] 5. The appellant 's right to sue survived against the respondent. The appellant having failed to bring on the record his legal representative within the period
4917: The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department of the State Government. They were promoted to the post of Executive Engineer and then to the post Deputy Executive Engineer. In the year 1976, the age of retirement was raised from 55 to 58 years in 1976, which was increased to 55 by a notification dated October 29, 1976. The petitioners challenged the said notification on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The State contended that the age of superannuation was raised from 60 to 58 years and that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the Government was estopped from reducing the age of retirement to 55, since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age of Retirement to 55; that the decision of the Government was bad for non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of fixing the age of reemployment; that the action of the Government in reducing the age was arbitrary and discriminatory; that the petitioners had no right to continue in service after attaining the age of 58 years, and that the decision taken by the Government was not based on any objective criteria or relevant considerations. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The decision of the State to reduce the age of compulsory retirement to 55 is not arbitrary but is based on an objective consideration of all relevant factors. [5B] 1.2 The decision of Government is not vitiated merely because it is based on irrelevant factors. It must be supported by reasons. [6C] 1.3 The decision of government is not immune from judicial review unless it suffers from arbitrariness, irrationality or perversity. [6D] 1.4 The decision of State to reduce age of retirement to 55 cannot be interfered with unless it is shown to be arbitrary or unreasonable. [6E] 1.5 The decision of this Court in State of Punjab vs N.K. Sharma, ; , relied upon.
6622: The appellant was a dealer in milk and milk products. He purchased certain goods from the respondent, who used them for sale to a place outside the State of Andhra Pradesh. The sales were effected by him in the course of interState trade or commerce. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on the turnover of sales made by the appellant. The Sales Tax Officer held that the appellant had not sold the goods at all and therefore he was liable to pay sales tax under section 9(1) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Sales Tax Officer. In further appeal the Tribunal held that the sales were not taxable under section 9 (2) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The High Court dismissed the petition filed by the appellant under article 226 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso added to sub section (2) by the Amendment Act of 1973 is not compatible with the provisions of section 5 of the Central Act. [353B] 2. The proviso does not take away the right of the State Government to levy sales tax on transactions of purchase of goods which are specified in Schedule B. [354C] 3. The proviso is not intended to confer any new right on the dealers. It merely clarifies the position. [355D] 4. The proviso cannot be construed as an exception to the main provision. [356E] 5. The proviso has been inserted by the Amendment of 1973 with effect from 9.4.1979. The proviso must be read along with the main provision and it is not necessary to go into the question whether the proviso is complai nate or supplementary to the main enactment. [357F G] 6. The proviso applies only if the transaction is one of sale of goods. [358A] 7. The proviso should not be so interpreted as to make it redundant. [359G] 8. The proviso would have no application where the transaction is of sale of the goods specified in Schedule A. [360H; 361A]
1329: The appellant, a firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act, was carrying on business in cotton and castor oil. In its return of turnover for the period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1955, it claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of sales of cotton of the total value of Rs. 68,493 2 6 and sales of castor oil of the total amount of Rs. 6,47,509 1 6 as mentioned above. The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The appellant 's appeal against that order was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the goods were not "a person " within the meaning of article 286 (1)(b). The High Court in second appeal affirmed the decision of the appellate authority. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods remained their property till they crossed the customs frontier and therefore, the sale must be deemed to have taken place "in the course of export" and that the sales must be held to have been effected at some point of time before shipment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The words " a person " in section 10( b) of the Act are wide enough to include a dealer who is a "registered dealer ". [639 C] The word "registered" does not mean only a person who has been registered but includes a person who is merely a "dealer". [640 E] The word 'registered ' means a person who carries on business or has his principal place of business in India. It cannot be said that the goods passed to the buyers on shipment. If the goods had crossed the customs barrier and they were sold there, then the sale would be an "sale" within the meaning Of article 286(1)(b) of Constitution. [641 A B]
3893: The appellant divorced her husband in 1965. She was living with her parents and a daughter. In the year 1962, she filed an application for maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for a monthly allowance for the son and Rs. 400/ for the mother. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the appellant was a divorce and therefore ineligible for maintenance. The respondent moved the Sessions Judge under section 125, Cr. P.C., for a monthly payment of Rs. 300/ for the son, and Rs.400/ for the father for their subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay, where the parties lived, was high. The Sessions Judge dismissed the revision petition. The High Court allowed the appeal. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code is not intended to be exhaustive or exhaustive. It only provides that a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband shall be entitled to claim maintenance from her husband. [501H; 502A B] (2) The Explanation does not contemplate any specific plea based upon the latter provision, set up anywhere in the courts below or urged before us. The Explanation does provide that a woman whose marriage is subsisting on the date of commencement of the Act, shall be entitled for maintenance from her former husband if he had been divorced by him before such commencement. [510B C] (3) The Explanation is not intended as a rule of evidence but is merely a rule of caution. The Explanation is meant to clarify the meaning of the expression 'wife ' occurring in the Explanation. [511D E]
5888: The appellant was a licensee of the country liquor shop. 6521: The appellant was the tenant of a shop in item 17 (2) of the property set out in Schedule A to the plaint. The respondent had also let out the same premises to another person. The respondent was in arrears. The appellant was entitled to recover the arrears of rent. The respondent has denied that the appellant ever sublet the premises. The respondent did not deny that the appellant has sublet the premises or any part thereof. [544G H] 3.1 The appellant was not entitled to
6647: The petitioners were granted a licence in terms of para 176 of the Import Policy 1978 79 for an amount to be calculated at one third the flexibility in value terms of Rs.10 lakhs, whichever is less. The petitioners had imported certain items which were excluded under the Import Policy, 1978 79 and were not only prohibited from importing items which were included in Appendices 1 Part A, 3 Part B and 5 Part A subject to the following conditions: (a) that the c.i.f. value of a `single item ' on the basis of 10% as at (a) above, works out to less than Rupees one lakh, import would be permitted upto a value of Rs.1 lakh; (b) that the import of items appearing in Appendions 1 Part A and 8 shall not exceed 10% of the flexability allowed on the licence; and (c) that the additional licences issued to Export Houses will also be valid for the import of the following items: (i) Export House Certificates to be issued by the Export House in respect of the export of the products manufactured by the Export Houses. (ii) Additional licences issued to the Export House for import of the products mentioned in Append Nos. 1 Part A to 8. (iii) Import of items appearing against Appendices I Part A and 9. (iv) Import of non OGL capital goods (other than those appearing in Appdts. 1 Part B and 8) without indigenous clearance, subject to the same conditions as stipulated at (ii) above, within the overall flexibility allowed on the Licence. The petitioners contended that sub para (10) of para 218 of the Import policy 1988 1991 was discriminatory inasmuch as it discriminated between Export Houses who had imported items which were exempted from importation under para 176 of Import Policy 1988 1991 79 and those who had imported item which were exempt from importation. It was further submitted that sub para(10) of Para 218 was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right to carry on trade or business guaranteed by article 19(g). Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to succeed. [213B]
6157: The appellant, a manufacturer of fusel oil, was manufacturing fusel and other products. It had supplied the goods to its customers on payment of price in drums/containers supplied by the buyer. The appellant claimed that the value of the drums should be included in the assessable value of the goods as the appellant had not supplied the containers at their factory gate. The Assistant Collector held that the value should have been included in the value of drums supplied by the appellant. The Tribunal upheld the contention of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the question whether for determining the assessable value the value of such drums or containers provided by its customer (the assessee) would also have to be excluded from the assessable value, was not one which could be determined only by reference to the drum content of the drum but by reference to its density and quality. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The dramatic content of the product is not merely the resultant of the drama but the durability of the drags and the dramatic effect of the dragging process. [439E] 2.1. If the dramate is not supplied by the customer at his own cost, the value of these dramates cannot be included in its assessable value. [440A B] 2.2. The drums are not delivered at the factory gate but at the factory premises. They are sent out from the factory gate to the factory gate. There is no reason why the dramatine should be treated as the dramae. [443C D] 3.1. In the instant case, the dramatirel is not delivered at any place other than the factory gate, nor is it sent out from any other place. The dromation of the daram is not done at the factory door. The dummy drams are sent out at the factory of the appellant and are sent out to the factory of its customers. The drum is not sent out at all. The dumb drams do not come within the definition of "drug"
6413: The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) read with section 161 I.P.C. and section 161 I, P.C. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. On 6.10, 1975 he received a money from PW 1 for the purchase of a canteen. The appellant had taken food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued the practice before the notice was issued. The appellant returned the amount due to him and there had been no demand for a bribe as there had been a demand for a sum of Rs. 100/ for the supply of the canteen. The recovery of the currency notes from the appellant was not challenged. The Trial Court accepted the plea of the appellant that PW 1 had returned the amount but held that the presumption under section 4 is rebutted. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the appellant had a consistent case even from the earliest opportunity that the currency notes found in his possession were the money returned by PW 1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appellant and the presumption under Section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanation offered by the appellant was reasonable and probable. 3442: The appellant 's application under section 18 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, for registration of a public trust was dismissed by the Charity Commissioner on the ground that the Sansthan had not been registered as a private trust. The High Court held that the appellant 's evidence showed that the Sanathan had acquired certain properties and the said property was used by the public for the purpose of the temple. HELD: (1) The High Court failed to consider all the material documentary evidence produced on behalf of appellant. [801 G] (2) The High court has misread the evidence and overlooked the fact that the Sanwardhas were appointed attorneys of the appellant 'Sankarrao Deshpunde and Ramkrishna Tryambak Deshpanrao. 2035: The appellants were workmen of the Bombay Port Trust, who were and have been represented by the Trustees first introduced a two shift system of work in the Alexandra Docks on June 30, 1953. The appellants were employed as watchmen in the Bombay Port Trusts. They were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 100 per day for each of the shift. The appellants claimed that they had worked for 8 hours a day and that there was no breach of the provisions of the Act. The Trustees contended that the existing system of work required any modification. The Tribunal held that the existing practice was not to get hours ' overtime and rejected the demand. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Tribunal had erred in holding that the existing method of working was only one of the methods of working; (ii) the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was violation of the provisions contained in section 25F(b) of the Act; (iii) the Tribunal could not have fixed rest hours at the Alexander Docks because the same system was continued throughout the year and the same system had been extended to the Prince 's and Victoria Docks on December 15, 1953. HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that in regard to any scheduled employment minimum rates of wages in respect of which have been fixed under the Act, the appropriate Government may fix different rates of wages for different classes of employees or different classes of persons. [635 B] (2) The Tribunal has rightly held that the practice was not contrary to law. [636 C] (3) The Tribunal had correctly come to the conclusion that the existing procedure was not contrary. [637 E] (4) The Tribunal should have given reasons for its conclusions. [638 F] (5) The Tribunal is justified in holding that it was not correct in holding that a change in the system of work was necessary. [639 G]

784: The appellant was granted a lease of the mines in respect of certain lands. The lease deed provided that the lessee would be entitled to receive compensation for the loss caused by the termination of the lease and that the lessee shall not be liable to pay any compensation for the period during which the termination took place. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease, but the Collector rejected it on the ground that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was for a period exceeding one year, it could only be terminated without compensation under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Collector. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant 's right to hold the land was not affected by the provisions of sub section (2) of section 20 of the Abolition of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant 's rights created before the notified date were not enforceable against the Government by reason of section 20(2) of the Act, because the lease was not for a term exceeding one year but was for a term of one year. [801 G] (ii) The appellant was not entitled to the protection of article 31(2) Of the Constitution. [802 B D] (iii) The appellant could not claim to have any right to the land in question. [803 C] (iv) The appellant had no right to the leasehold rights which were created prior to July 1. 1945. The appellant could therefore not claim to be entitled to the benefit of the third proviso to section 19(2) which provides for compensation for the breach of the terms of the lease. [804 A B] (v) The appellant cannot claim to have a right to the property in dispute. [805 E]
